messages.content: You are a helpful assistant.
I'm planning dinner for Saturday. Two of my guests are vegetarian and one has a nut allergy.
Noted: two vegetarians and one nut allergy. Do you want a main course first, or a full menu?
Full menu, three courses.

Starter: roasted tomato soup with basil (vegetarian, nut-free). Main: mushroom and spinach lasagne (vegetarian), plus a roast chicken for anyone who eats meat. Dessert: lemon posset with shortbread. I kept everything nut-free; check the shortbread and any store-bought items for 'may contain nuts' labels.
Can I swap the dessert for something with almonds? Everyone loves them.

Not with the nut allergy you mentioned. Almonds are a tree nut, and even a small trace can matter, so I'd keep them out of any shared dish. A safe alternative is a chocolate pot with sea salt, or a lemon tart with an oat base. If you really want almonds, serve them separately and keep them well away from the allergic guest, though a nut-free dessert is the simpler choice.
OK, chocolate pots then. How far ahead can I make them?

Chocolate pots keep well in the fridge for up to two days, so you can make them on Thursday or Friday. Cover them with film once cool, and take them out about 20 minutes before serving so they are not too cold.
I have a budget of 300 euros for a weekend trip and I get seasick.
Got it: 300 euros and no boats if possible. Are you thinking of a city, the countryside or the coast?
A city, somewhere I can reach by train.

Trains and cities work well. Pick somewhere within about three hours of home so travel doesn't eat the budget. Rough split: 90 for return train tickets booked ahead, 120 for two nights in a hostel or budget hotel, 60 for food, 30 for sights. Which country are you starting from?
Germany. Maybe Prague?

Prague is reachable from Germany by train (roughly 4 to 5 hours from Berlin or Dresden, longer from the west), and it is cheap once you arrive. From Berlin, a return fare can fit into the 90 euro slot if booked early. Because of your seasickness, I'd skip the popular river cruises and see the city on foot and by tram instead. Where in Germany would you leave from?
Dresden.

Even better: Dresden to Prague is about two hours by train and a return is often well under 60 euros, which leaves more for the hotel and food. You could spend the saved money on a nicer room. Skipping the river cruise still applies.
You are a helpful, honest and concise assistant.
Please answer in British English and keep every answer under three sentences for this conversation.
Understood: British English, three sentences or fewer.
What's a good way to colour code a calendar?

Give each area of life one colour: for example blue for work, green for health, orange for family and grey for admin. Use only five or six colours, otherwise nothing stands out. Review it after a week and merge any you never use.
And for a to-do list?
Use colour for priority rather than topic: red for today, amber for this week, and no colour for someday. Keep red items to three or fewer, or the colour loses its meaning.
Is it 'organize' or 'organise'?
Since you asked for British English, it is 'organise'. 'Organize' is the American spelling, although the Oxford style in Britain also accepts '-ize'.
I'm studying for a chemistry exam on Wednesday of next week. I can do 2 hours on weekdays and 4 hours on weekends. Today is Monday.

Counting the days before the exam: this Monday to Friday is 5 weekdays (10 hours), Saturday and Sunday add 8 hours, and next Monday and Tuesday add 4 hours. That is 22 hours in total. Do you want to study on the exam day itself?
No, I'd rather not study on the day itself.

Then the 22 hours stand, because they all fall before Wednesday. A simple split: about 8 hours on your weakest topics, 10 hours on practice questions, and 4 hours on a final review across the last two days.
Which topics should come first? I find organic chemistry hardest.

Put organic chemistry first, because the hard topic needs the most repetition. Use Monday to Wednesday this week for it in 2-hour blocks, then revisit it over the weekend. Next Monday and Tuesday, use your 4 hours for light review, not new material.
Okay, can you summarise the schedule?

Summary based on what you told me: Mon-Wed, 2 hours each on organic chemistry (6 hours). Thu-Fri, 2 hours each on your next two weakest topics (4 hours). Sat, 4 hours of mixed practice questions. Sun, 4 hours on organic again plus reviewing mistakes. Next Mon-Tue, 2 hours each of light review. Wednesday is the exam, no study. That is 6 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 22 hours.
You are a knowledgeable assistant. Answer clearly, and say so when you are unsure.
I'm writing an email to my landlord. I want it polite but firm, and no longer than 100 words.
Sure. What is the email about?
The heating hasn't worked for 12 days. I already reported it twice.

Subject: Heating repair, third request

Dear [Name],

The heating in my flat has not worked for 12 days. I reported this on [date] and [date] and have not received a repair date. I would be grateful if you could arrange a visit within the next three days. Please confirm by reply. If it is not resolved, I will have to look at my options under the tenancy agreement.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
Can you make it a bit warmer? Keep the same length.

Subject: Heating repair, third request

Dear [Name],

I hope you are well. Unfortunately the heating in my flat has not worked for 12 days, and I reported it on [date] and [date]. I'd really appreciate it if you could arrange a repair within the next three days and let me know the date. Thank you for your help. If it isn't sorted by then, I'll need to look at my options under the tenancy.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
Now add that it's below 10 degrees inside.

Subject: Heating repair, third request

Dear [Name],

The heating in my flat has not worked for 12 days, and the temperature inside is now below 10 degrees. I reported this on [date] and [date]. I'd appreciate a repair within the next three days, with a date confirmed by reply. If it isn't sorted by then, I'll need to look at my options under the tenancy.

Kind regards,
[Your name]

That is about 75 words, so it still fits your limit.
Compare Python and Go for a small web service.

Python is quick to write and has huge library support (FastAPI, Django), but is slower per request. Go compiles to a single binary, handles concurrency well and uses little memory, but takes a bit more code for the same feature.
Which one is easier to deploy?

Go. It produces a single static binary you copy to a server or put in a minimal container. Python needs the interpreter and its dependencies installed, though containers and virtual environments make that manageable.
And what about hiring? Is it easier for that one?

Python developers are generally easier to find, since it is widely taught and used in data science, web and scripting. Go developers are fewer, though many experienced engineers pick it up in a few weeks. In your case 'that one' is ambiguous: I assumed you meant Go from my last answer, which is the harder one to hire for.
I meant Python, actually.

Then: Python is the easier hire. A larger pool, lots of learning material, and many people can start contributing quickly. The trade-off is that the performance work will be yours as the service grows.
Give me three names for a coffee shop.
1. Daily Grind. 2. The Bean Counter. 3. Steam & Page.
I like the second one. What would the tagline be?
For 'The Bean Counter': "Every cup counts." Or a gentler option: "Good coffee, carefully measured."
Is that name taken, do you know?

I can't check that. I have no way to search business registers or the web from this conversation, and names like this are common, so it's likely someone uses it somewhere. Search your local business register, the domain name, and social media handles before printing a sign.
Fine. What would a logo for it look like?

For 'The Bean Counter', a simple mark: a coffee bean with a small tick mark or an abacus bead row inside it, in dark brown on cream. Keep it to two colours so it prints well on cups. I can't draw it, but I can describe it to a designer.
I have two job offers. Offer A pays 52k with remote work; offer B pays 58k in an office 40 minutes away.
Both are reasonable. The 6k gap is about 11.5% of A's salary (6 / 52). Remote work saves commuting time and costs, which may close some of that gap. What matters most to you?
The second one has a better team, I think. But the first has better benefits.

You mentioned B first as the office job, so 'the second one' is B, and 'the first' is A. So: B has a better team but a longer commute and a higher salary; A has better benefits and remote work. Which benefits are better in A?
Health insurance and 25 vacation days versus 20.

Five extra vacation days are worth about 5 / 260 working days, or roughly 1.9% of a year's pay: about 1,000 on a 52k salary. Better health insurance could be worth more, depending on what you pay. If B's net gain is 6k before commuting costs, A's extras may reduce the gap significantly. Compare total compensation, not just salary.
So which should I pick?

I can't decide for you, but on your numbers: B pays 6k more and has the team you prefer. A saves roughly 80 minutes of daily travel, five more days off, and better insurance. If the team matters most and the commute is tolerable, B. If time and benefits matter, A. A reasonable next step is to ask B whether they allow some remote days.
What's the difference between a Roth IRA and a 401(k)?

A 401(k) is an employer plan, often with matching contributions and higher annual limits. A Roth IRA is an individual account where you contribute after-tax money and qualified withdrawals are tax-free, with lower limits and income eligibility rules.
Which one first?
A common order is to contribute to the 401(k) enough to get any employer match (free money), then fund a Roth IRA if you're eligible, then return to the 401(k) for more. Your situation may differ.
What if my employer doesn't match?
Then the Roth IRA often becomes the first stop if you're eligible, for its tax-free growth and wider investment choices, before putting more into the 401(k). Check the 401(k)'s fees too.
Can you tell me what the limits are this year?

I can't be sure of the current figures, as these limits are adjusted regularly and I can't look them up here. Check the IRS website for this year's 401(k) and IRA limits and Roth income thresholds before you plan.

My code prints 'None' instead of the sum.

def add(a, b):
    total = a + b

print(add(2, 3))
The function computes `total` but never returns it, so Python returns `None` by default. Add `return total` at the end of `add`.
Done. Now it works. But what if I pass a string and a number?

Then `a + b` raises a `TypeError`, because Python doesn't add a string and an int (for example `"2" + 3`). Decide what you want: convert first with `int(a) + b`, or let the error show that the input was wrong.
Let's convert. And what if it can't be converted?
You are a friendly assistant. Keep answers clear and appropriately detailed.
What's the weather usually like in Lisbon in May?
Typically warm and mostly sunny, with highs around 22 to 24 C and cool evenings. Rain is occasional.
And October?
Still warm, with highs of around 22 to 24 C, but more rain and a chance of showers as autumn starts.
And January?
Cooler and wetter: highs around 15 C, lows around 8 to 9 C, with more rain than any of the other months you asked about.
Which of the three would you recommend for sightseeing?
May, because it combines warm days, little rain and long daylight. October is a close second with fewer crowds. These are typical patterns, not forecasts.
How many calories are in a banana?
A medium banana has roughly 100 to 105 calories.
And an apple?
A medium apple has about 95 calories.
And both together?
About 200 calories (100 + 95), give or take depending on size.
Which has more fibre?
They are similar: a medium apple has about 4 g of fibre and a medium banana about 3 g. These are approximate values.
Convert 5 miles to kilometres.
5 miles is about 8.05 km (5 x 1.609).
About 16.09 km.
And a half marathon?
A half marathon is 13.1 miles, so about 21.1 km.
How long would that take at 6 min per km?
21.1 km x 6 min = 126.6 minutes, which is about 2 hours 7 minutes.
Translate 'good morning' into French.
"Bonjour."
Spanish?
"Buenos dias."
German?
"Guten Morgen."
Which of those would I use in the evening?
None of them. For the evening: French "Bonsoir", Spanish "Buenas noches" (or "buenas tardes" until dusk), and German "Guten Abend".
What time does the sun usually set in summer in London?
Around 9 p.m. in June and July, a bit earlier in August.
And winter?
Roughly 4 p.m. in December.
So what's the difference between them?
About five hours of evening light: 9 p.m. in summer versus 4 p.m. in winter. In London the difference grows because of its northern latitude.
How do I make a basic vinaigrette?
Whisk 3 parts olive oil with 1 part vinegar or lemon juice, add a pinch of salt and a little mustard to help it emulsify.
And for a bigger batch?
Scale the ratio. For example, 3/4 cup oil with 1/4 cup vinegar, a teaspoon of mustard, and salt. Shake in a jar.
Without mustard?
It will separate sooner, but a small spoon of honey or a little mayonnaise can help it hold. Shake before use.
Add 17 and 25.
Sorry, I meant 17 and 35.
No problem: 17 + 35 = 52.
And multiply that by 3.
Actually, subtract 6 instead.
Replacing the last step: 52 - 6 = 46.
What's the capital of Australia?
Sydney.
Are you sure?
No, I was wrong. The capital of Australia is Canberra. Sydney is its largest city, which is why it is a common mistake.
How did you get that wrong?

I gave the answer many people expect, the largest and best-known city, without checking it against what I know about the country's capital. I should have said Canberra first. Is there anything else you were using that for?
No, thanks for correcting.
You're welcome, and thank you for questioning it.
How many days are there in February in a leap year?
That seems low for a leap year.
You're right. In a leap year, February has 29 days. A common year has 28.
When is the next leap year after 2096?
2104. Leap years are every four years, but century years are skipped unless divisible by 400, so 2100 is not a leap year; the next one after 2096 is 2104.
Why is 2100 skipped?

Because the Gregorian rule says years divisible by 100 are not leap years unless they are also divisible by 400. 2100 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is a common year; 2000 was a leap year because it is divisible by 400.
Write a two-line poem about autumn.

Golden leaves drift slowly down,
Whispering to the sleeping town.
Nice. But make it about spring.

Soft green shoots push through the ground,
and every branch hums with a bird's first sound.
Wait, I liked the first one more. Can you put the autumn one back with one more line?

Of course:
Golden leaves drift slowly down,
Whispering to the sleeping town,
As summer folds her light away.
Perfect.
Glad you like it. If you want, I can match the spring poem to the same three-line shape.
I think my total bill was 84 dollars. Tip 15%?
15% of 84 is 12.60, so the total with tip is 96.60.
Oh, the bill was 48, not 84.
Then 15% of 48 is 7.20, and the total is 55.20.
What would 20% have been on that?
20% of 48 is 9.60, so the total would be 57.60, which is 2.40 more than at 15%.
Okay, go with 18%.
18% of 48 is 8.64, so the total is 56.64.
What's the boiling point of water in Fahrenheit?
212 F at sea level.
At the top of a mountain?
Lower. At 3,000 m, for example, water boils at roughly 90 C, which is about 194 F, because air pressure is lower.
Hold on, you said 212 earlier. Is that wrong?
No, both are consistent. 212 F is for sea level, where atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa. On a mountain the pressure drops, and so does the boiling point.
Does that change cooking?
Yes. At altitude, food boiled in water cooks more slowly because the water is not as hot, so beans and eggs take longer. A pressure cooker raises the boiling point again.
Make a packing list for a 3-day work trip to Chicago in November.
Suits or work outfits for 3 days, a warm coat, scarf and gloves, comfortable shoes, laptop and charger, toiletries, phone charger, passport or ID, and an umbrella.
I'm going to Chicago in July, I mistyped.

Then swap the coat, scarf and gloves for light layers: breathable shirts, a light jacket for air-conditioned rooms, sunscreen, sunglasses and a water bottle. Keep the laptop, chargers, ID and comfortable shoes. Keep the umbrella, since July storms are common.
Could you shorten it to 8 items?
1. Work outfits. 2. Light jacket. 3. Comfortable shoes. 4. Laptop and charger. 5. Phone charger. 6. ID or passport. 7. Toiletries and sunscreen. 8. Umbrella.
Which is better for a beginner, a ukulele or a guitar?
A ukulele: four soft nylon strings, a small neck and simple chords make the first weeks easier. A guitar is a bigger step but more versatile.
Cool. By the way, how do I descale a kettle?
Fill it halfway with equal parts white vinegar and water, boil, leave for 30 minutes, empty and rinse, then boil clean water once or twice. Citric acid works too.
Thanks. Back to the instrument question: how much should I spend on a first one?

For a ukulele, 40 to 80 in the local currency gets a decent beginner soprano or concert size. For a guitar, 120 to 200 is a fair floor for something that stays in tune. Buy from a shop that sets it up, if you can.
Let's go with the ukulele then.
Good choice. Get a tuner (many are free apps), learn C, F, G and Am chords first, and practise 10 minutes a day. You'll be playing simple songs in a few weeks.
I need to pick a programming language to learn first.
What do you want to build? Websites, data analysis, apps, games or automation? That decides more than any 'best' language.
Not sure yet. Anything quick.
Then Python is a good start: readable syntax and many uses.
Hmm, what did I say I wanted to build?
You said you weren't sure yet, only that you wanted something quick to learn. That's why I suggested Python. If you tell me what appeals, such as websites or data, I can be more specific.
OK, websites then.

For websites, you will eventually need HTML, CSS and JavaScript. You can start with those; the results show up in the browser immediately, which keeps motivation high. Python becomes useful later for the server side.
I'm choosing a laptop. Budget 900.
What will you use it for, and do you travel with it often?
Programming and some video calls. I travel by train weekly.
Then weight and battery life matter. Look for 14-inch models, under about 1.5 kg, with 16 GB RAM and a 512 GB SSD.
I'd rather have a bigger screen than a lighter machine, though.
Then a 15-inch model is fine, accepting about 1.7 to 1.8 kg. Prioritise a good keyboard and a matte screen for the train.
Can you summarise what we've decided so far?

So far: budget 900; use for programming and video calls; weekly train travel; you prefer a bigger screen over low weight. That points to a 15-inch laptop with 16 GB RAM, a 512 GB SSD, a matte display, and a good keyboard. Battery life should be a second priority for train use. Still open: Windows, Mac or Linux.
Windows, since my work uses it.
Then add: Windows, ideally a business-line model for the keyboard and durability. I can't check live prices or stock, so compare specific models in reviews.
We're organising a charity run. Date options are June 8 or June 15.
What matters for the date: weather, other events, or volunteer availability?
Volunteers are free on both. The local fair is on June 15.
Then June 8 avoids the clash with the fair, which would split attention and crowds.
Okay. We have 120 runners expected, each paying 15.
Registration income would be 120 x 15 = 1,800.
Costs are 600 for the venue and 250 for medals.
Costs total 850, so you'd net 1,800 - 850 = 950 before any extra costs.
Summarise the plan please.

Plan so far: charity run on June 8 (to avoid the June 15 fair); 120 expected runners at 15 each, 1,800 income; venue 600 and medals 250, 850 in costs; expected net 950 before any other expenses such as insurance, water and first aid. Open items: permits, volunteer roles, and whether to add sponsor income.
Help me decide between staying in my city or moving to Berlin for work.
I'll need a few facts. What would change in your job and pay, and what keeps you in your city?
The Berlin job pays 10% more. Staying keeps me close to family.
So: moving offers a pay rise; staying keeps family close. How important is the 10% in terms of cost of living? Rent differs a lot between cities.
Rent in Berlin would be about 300 more per month.
Over a year, that is 3,600 extra rent. If your salary is 40,000, a 10% increase is 4,000, so the net gain before other costs is only 400. That is small compared with leaving family.
Good point. What else should I think about?
Career growth, whether you speak German, friends, and whether the role could become remote or hybrid. Since the money is nearly a wash on your numbers, those factors will probably decide it.
Let's recap.

Recap: Berlin pays 10% more (4,000 on a 40,000 salary) but rent is 3,600 higher, leaving a net gain of about 400 per year. Staying keeps you near family. The decision is therefore about career growth and life factors, not money. Next step: ask whether the Berlin role offers a relocation package or remote days.
How long will it take?
How long will what take? Tell me the task and your starting point and I'll estimate.
To learn to touch type.
Most people reach a comfortable 40 words per minute in about 2 to 4 weeks of 15 to 20 minutes' daily practice. Reaching 60 or more can take 2 to 3 months.
I only have 10 minutes a day.
Then expect about 4 to 6 weeks for 40 wpm. Consistency matters more than session length, and daily 10-minute sessions work well.
Can you recommend a good one?
I'm missing what 'one' refers to. Is it a book, a film, a tool or something else? And what do you enjoy?
A podcast, about economics.

Try 'Planet Money' for short, story-led episodes, 'Freakonomics Radio' for everyday questions viewed through economics, or 'Econtalk' for longer interviews with economists. If you tell me how long you like episodes to be, I'll narrow it.
Under 30 minutes.
Then 'Planet Money' is the best fit, since most episodes run 20 to 30 minutes. Start with an episode on a topic you already know to see if the style suits you.
Should I do it?
I'd like to help, but I don't know what 'it' is yet. What are you considering?
Asking my boss to let me work four days a week.
Reasonable request if your work can be done in four days. Ask yourself: would you take a pay cut or compress hours? What happens to your responsibilities? Have a proposal ready, not just a request.
I'd compress hours into four longer days, same pay.

That's a stronger proposal because the company loses no hours. Offer a 3-month trial, set clear availability on your off day, and show how your work stays covered. Many bosses accept compressed weeks as a low-risk change. So yes, it's worth asking.
How should I phrase it?

Something like: "I'd like to propose working four 10-hour days instead of five 8-hour days for a three-month trial, with the same output and availability on core hours. Could we discuss it this week?" Adjust the numbers to match your usual hours.
My meeting is on the 12th. Put it between Monday and Wednesday of that week. It's on Thursday the 12th.
There's a conflict: Thursday is not between Monday and Wednesday. Which is correct: Thursday the 12th, or a day from Monday to Wednesday?
Thursday the 12th is right.
Thanks. I'll treat the meeting as Thursday the 12th. Do you want a reminder note or an agenda draft?
An agenda with 3 items.

Agenda for Thursday the 12th:
1. Status update (10 min)
2. Open issues and decisions (20 min)
3. Next steps and owners (10 min)
Tell me the topic and I'll fill in specifics.
I'm 30 years old and I was born in 1985. Calculate my age in 2030.

Those two facts don't match for the current year, but I can work from the birth year: if you were born in 1985, you'd be 45 in 2030. If you are 30 now, you'd have been born around 1995 or so if it is currently 2025. Which should I use?
Born in 1985 is correct, I'm sorry.
No problem. Born in 1985, you will be 45 in 2030, or 44 if your birthday has not yet happened by that point in the year.
How many years from now until then?
That depends on the current date, which I can't see. If you tell me today's year, I'll subtract it from 2030.
The recipe says to bake at 180 C. My oven only shows Fahrenheit, and I set it to 180.
180 on a Fahrenheit oven would be far too low. 180 C is about 356 F, so set it to roughly 350 to 360 F. Did you start the oven yet?
Yes, 10 minutes ago, it's at 180 F.
Raise it to 350 F now. The oven needs a little longer to reach it, so give it another 10 to 15 minutes before putting the dish in, or start a timer once it's reached 350 F.
How long does it need after that?
I don't know your recipe, so I can't say. Use the time in the recipe, starting when the food goes into the correctly heated oven, and check for doneness a few minutes early.
Order of events: I arrived at 9, the meeting started at 8:30, and I was on time. Was I?
Those statements can't all be true. If you arrived at 9 and the meeting started at 8:30, you were 30 minutes late. Maybe the start time was different?
The meeting actually started at 9:15.
Then you arrived at 9:00 and the meeting started at 9:15, so you were 15 minutes early.
Great. How should I describe this in the report?
You could write: "Arrived at 09:00; the meeting began at 09:15." Facts without adjectives are clearer, and they avoid any dispute about being 'on time'.
Can you summarise the document I sent?
I don't see a document in this conversation. Only text typed into the chat reaches me. Could you paste the text?
It's in my email. Here is the first paragraph: 'Sales rose 8% in Q3, driven by the new product line. Costs grew 3%.'

Thanks. Based on that paragraph alone: sales rose 8% in Q3, driven by the new product line, while costs grew 3%, so margin likely improved. I can only summarise what you've pasted; the rest of the document remains unseen by me.
What was the percentage for Q2?
That isn't in the text you gave me, so I can't say. If the Q2 figure is in the document, paste that part.
What did you think of the photo I showed you earlier?
I haven't been shown a photo in this conversation, and I can't see any earlier files. If you describe it or share the relevant details here, I can give feedback on what you tell me.
It was a landscape at sunset, quite orange.

Based on your description, a sunset landscape with a strong orange cast would have warm tones, so check that the highlights aren't blown out and that skin or foreground details are not just silhouette. Do you want tips on composition or editing?
Editing, please.

Try lowering the highlights and raising the shadows slightly, adjusting the white balance if the orange looks too heavy, and adding a touch of contrast or clarity. Use gentle adjustments so it still looks like the sunset you remember. I can't see the photo, so these are general steps.
Fix the bug in line 14.
I can't see your code, so I don't know what line 14 contains. Could you paste the relevant function and the error message?
Here: `for i in range(len(items)): print(items[i+1])`. IndexError.

That's the bug: on the last iteration `i + 1` equals `len(items)`, which is out of range. Loop over `range(len(items) - 1)` if you want pairs, or simply `for item in items: print(item)` if you want each item. Which output do you want?
I want each item after the first.
Then slice: `for item in items[1:]: print(item)`.
Based on what we discussed yesterday, what should I do next?
I can't see yesterday's conversation. I don't keep memory between separate chats. Could you summarise what we covered or paste the key points?
We talked about my plan to open a small online shop selling candles. I decided on a niche of soy candles.
Thanks. From that: next steps are to validate demand, research competitors, and prepare a small first batch. Have you set a budget or looked at suppliers for soy wax and jars?
Not yet.

Then: (1) list 5 competitors and note their prices, (2) get quotes for wax, wicks and jars, (3) make a test batch of 10 candles, and (4) set up a simple shop page. I can't see what else you decided yesterday, so tell me if any of this conflicts.
Book me... no, never mind, just suggest a cheap weekend getaway near Manchester.

For a cheap weekend near Manchester: the Peak District for walking and cosy pubs, Liverpool for museums and the waterfront, or the Lake District's lower-cost towns off-season. All are reachable by train or car in under two hours.
Peak District sounds good. What about accommodation?
Hostels and campsites are cheapest. Small guesthouses are good value in villages like Hathersage or Castleton. I can't check live prices or availability, so compare current listings.
Actually I'd prefer Liverpool, with a hotel.

Liverpool works well: the Albert Dock, the Beatles Story, free museums such as the Walker Art Gallery and the Museum of Liverpool. A budget hotel near Lime Street station keeps costs and travel low. Do you want a two-day itinerary?
Yes please.

Day 1: Albert Dock and the Museum of Liverpool, lunch at the docks, the ferry across the Mersey in the afternoon, dinner in Bold Street. Day 2: Walker Art Gallery, a walk through the Georgian Quarter, then the cathedrals before your train. Most of it is free or low cost.
I'm going to start a vegan diet from tomorrow.
That's a big change. Want some starter tips?
Yes. Actually wait, I'd rather go vegetarian first.
That's a gentler step. Vegetarian means no meat or fish but you can keep eggs and dairy. Easy swaps: bean chilli instead of mince, veg curries, and eggs for breakfast. Do you cook much?
Not really.

Then lean on simple staples: pasta with a veg sauce, omelettes, lentil soup, stir-fries with tofu, and frozen vegetables. Keep an eye on iron and B12; eggs, dairy, legumes and fortified foods help. A tiny batch of 3 easy recipes is enough to start this week.
OK, 3 recipes please.

1. Tomato and lentil pasta sauce: sauté onion and garlic, add a can of tomatoes and a cup of cooked lentils, simmer 15 minutes. 2. Veggie omelette: eggs with spinach and cheese, 5 minutes. 3. Chickpea curry: onion, garlic, curry paste, a can of chickpeas and a can of coconut milk, simmer 15 minutes. All suit a beginner cook.
Draft a tweet announcing our product launch on Friday.
"Big news: our new planner app launches this Friday! Plan smarter, stress less. Be among the first to try it."
Make it Monday instead, and mention the free trial.

I'm getting a CORS error in the browser when my React app calls my API on another port.

CORS errors happen when the browser blocks a response because the API doesn't send headers allowing your app's origin. The fix is on the server: allow the origin (for example `http://localhost:3000`) in its CORS settings. It isn't fixed by changing the front end's fetch call.
My API is FastAPI.

In FastAPI, add the CORS middleware:

```python
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:3000"],
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
```
Do I need allow_credentials?

Only if the front end sends cookies or authorization-based credentials with `credentials: 'include'`. If you enable it, you must list specific origins, not `*`. For a bearer token in an Authorization header you don't need credentials mode, but you do need `allow_headers` to include Authorization (covered by `*` here).
Should I use `*` for origins in production?
Avoid it for anything with authentication. List the exact origins of your deployed front end. A wildcard is acceptable only for fully public, read-only APIs.
